{{Use American English|date=January 2019}}
{{Short description|Stochastic process generalizing Brownian motion}}
{{Infobox probability distribution|name=Wiener Process|pdf_image=Wiener process with sigma.svg|mean={{math|0}}|variance=<math>\sigma^2 t</math>|type=multivariate}}[[File:wiener process zoom.png|thumb|300px|A single realization of a one-dimensional Wiener process]]
[[File:WienerProcess3D.svg|thumb|300px|A single realization of a three-dimensional Wiener process]]

In [[mathematics]], the '''Wiener process''' (or '''Brownian motion''', due to its historical connection with [[Brownian motion|the physical process of the same name]]) is a real-valued [[continuous-time]] [[stochastic process]] named after [[Norbert Wiener]].<ref>{{cite book |last= Dobrow|first=Robert |author-link= |date=2016 |title=Introduction to Stochastic Processes with R |publisher=Wiley |pages=321–322 |doi=10.1002/9781118740712 |bibcode=2016ispr.book.....D |url=https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/book/10.1002/9781118740712 |isbn=9781118740651}}</ref><ref>{{cite book |last=Wiener |first=Norbert |editor-last=Masani |editor-first=P. R. |year=1976 |title=Norbert Wiener: Collected Works with Commentaries |volume=1 |publisher=MIT Press |location=Cambridge, MA |isbn=978-0262230704}}</ref> It is one of the best known [[Lévy process]]es ([[càdlàg]] stochastic processes with [[stationary increments|stationary]] [[independent increments]]). It occurs frequently in pure and [[applied mathematics]], [[economy|economics]], [[quantitative finance]], [[evolutionary biology]], and [[physics]].

The Wiener process plays an important role in both pure and applied mathematics. In pure mathematics, the Wiener process gave rise to the study of continuous time [[martingale (probability theory)|martingale]]s. It is a key process in terms of which more complicated stochastic processes can be described. As such, it plays a vital role in [[stochastic calculus]], [[diffusion process]]es and even [[potential theory]]. It is the driving process of [[Schramm–Loewner evolution]]. In [[applied mathematics]], the Wiener process is used to represent the integral of a [[white noise]] [[Gaussian process]], and so is useful as a model of noise in [[electronics engineering]] (see [[Brownian noise]]), instrument errors in [[Filter (signal processing)|filtering theory]] and disturbances in [[control theory]].

The Wiener process has applications throughout the mathematical sciences. In physics, researchers use it to model Brownian motion and other types of diffusion, often through the [[Fokker–Planck equation|Fokker–Planck]] and [[Langevin equation]]s, which describe how random motion evolves over time. It also underpins the rigorous [[path integral formulation]] of [[quantum mechanics]]: by the [[Feynman–Kac formula]], one can represent solutions to the [[Schrödinger equation]] in terms of the Wiener process.<ref>{{cite book |author-link=Hagen Kleinert |last=Kleinert |first=Hagen |title=Path Integrals in Quantum Mechanics, Statistics, Polymer Physics, and Financial Markets |url=https://archive.org/details/pathintegralsinq0000klei |url-access=registration |edition=4th |publisher=World Scientific |location=Singapore |year=2004 |isbn=981-238-107-4 }}</ref> In [[physical cosmology]], it also appears in models of [[eternal inflation]]. The Wiener process is prominent in the [[mathematical finance|mathematical theory of finance]] as well, in particular the [[Black–Scholes]] option pricing model.<ref name=":0">{{cite book |last1=Karatsas |first1=Ioannis |last2=Shreve |first2=Steven E. |year=1998 |title=Brownian Motion and Stochastic Calculus |edition=2nd |publisher=[[Springer Science+Business Media|Springer]] |isbn=978-0-387-97655-6 |series=Graduate Texts in Mathematics |volume=113|language=|pages=103, 108, 110}}</ref> 

== Definitions ==

=== Canonical definition ===
The '''Wiener process''' {{math|''W''}} is a real-valued [[continuous-time]] [[stochastic process]] characterized by the following properties:<ref>{{cite book |last=Durrett |first=Rick |author-link=Rick Durrett |date=2019 |title=Probability: Theory and Examples |edition=5th |chapter=Brownian Motion |publisher=Cambridge University Press |isbn=9781108591034}}</ref>

# {{math|''W''<sub>0</sub> {{=}} 0}} almost surely.
# {{mvar|W}} has [[independent increments]]: for every {{math|''t'' > 0}}, the future increments <math display="inline">W_{t+u} - W_t,\, u > 0,</math> are independent of the past values {{math|''W<sub>s</sub>''}}, {{math|''s'' < ''t''}}. Equivalently, for every {{math|''t'' > 0}} and <math display="inline">u \ge 0</math>, the increment <math display="inline">W_{t+u} - W_t</math> is independent of the sigma-algebra <math display="inline">\mathcal{F}_t^B = \sigma(W_s : 0 \le s \le t)</math>.
# {{mvar|W}} has Gaussian increments: for all <math display="inline">u, t \ge 0</math>, <math display="inline">W_{t+u} - W_t \sim \mathcal N(0,u).</math> That is, a time step {{mvar|u}} results in an increment that is [[Normal distribution|normally distributed]] with mean 0 and variance {{mvar|u}}.
# {{mvar|W}} has almost surely continuous paths: {{math|''W<sub>t</sub>''}} is almost surely continuous in {{mvar|t}}.

That the process has independent increments means that if {{math|0 ≤ ''s''<sub>1</sub> < ''t''<sub>1</sub> ≤ ''s''<sub>2</sub> < ''t''<sub>2</sub>}} then {{math|''W''<sub>''t''<sub>1</sub></sub> − ''W''<sub>''s''<sub>1</sub></sub>}} and {{math|''W''<sub>''t''<sub>2</sub></sub> − ''W''<sub>''s''<sub>2</sub></sub>}} are independent random variables, and the similar condition holds for {{mvar|n}} increments. 

The '''Wiener measure''' is the [[Law (stochastic processes)|probability law]] of the Wiener process on the space of [[continuous function]]s {{math|''g''}} with {{math|1=''g''(0) = 0}} equipped with the [[Borel set|Borel σ-algebra]]. An integral with respect to the Wiener measure may be called a '''Wiener integral'''.

=== Lévy characterization ===
An alternative characterization of the Wiener process is the so-called ''Lévy characterization'': A continuous (local) [[martingale (probability theory)|martingale]] {{math|''W''}} with {{math|1=''W''<sub>0</sub> = 0}} is a Wiener process if and only if its [[quadratic variation]] is {{math|1=[''W'', ''W'']<sub>''t''</sub> = ''t''}} (which means that {{math|''W''<sub>''t''</sub><sup>2</sup> − ''t''}} is a (local) martingale).

=== Gaussian process characterization ===
The Wiener process can be equivalently defined as a [[Gaussian process]] <math>W_t</math>, that is, a stochastic process such that for every set of indices <math>t_1,\dots, t_n\geq 0</math>, the random vector <math>(W_{t_1},\dots,W_{t_n})</math> is [[Multivariate normal distribution|multivariate Gaussian]], which has continuous paths and such that for all <math>s,t\geq 0</math> it holds<ref name=":3" />

<math display="block">\begin{align}
&\operatorname E[W_t]=0, \\
&\mathrm{Cov}(W_t,W_s)=\operatorname E[W_sW_t] = \min(s,t).
\end{align}</math>

In particular, the law of <math>W</math> on the space of continuous functions (equipped with the Borel σ-algebra) is uniquely determined, which is the Wiener measure. 

=== Wiener representation ===
Wiener (1923) also gave a representation of a Brownian path in terms of a random [[Fourier series]]. If <math display="inline">\xi_n</math> are independent Gaussian variables with mean zero and variance one, then
<math display="block">W_t = \xi_0 t+ \sqrt{2}\sum_{n=1}^\infty \xi_n\frac{\sin \pi n t}{\pi n}</math>
and
<math display="block"> W_t = \sqrt{2} \sum_{n=1}^\infty \xi_n \frac{\sin \left(\left(n - \frac{1}{2}\right) \pi t\right)}{ \left(n - \frac{1}{2}\right) \pi} </math>
represent a Brownian motion on <math display="inline">[0,1]</math>. This representation can also be obtained using the [[Karhunen–Loève theorem]].

The scaled process
<math display="block">\sqrt{c}\,  W_{t/c}</math>
is a Brownian motion on <math display="inline">[0,c]</math>.

=== White noise representation ===
In the physics and engineering literature, Brownian motion is often defined (informally) as

<math display="block">W_t=\int_0^t\xi(s)\mathrm d s</math>

with the white noise process <math>\xi</math> satisfying for <math>t,s\geq 0</math>

<math display="block">\begin{align}
&\operatorname E[\xi(t)]=0, \\
&\operatorname E[\xi(t)\xi(s)]=\delta(t-s), 
\end{align}</math>

with the [[Dirac delta function|Dirac delta]] "function" <math>\delta</math>. However, as shown below, the paths of the Wiener process have unbounded variation and, thus, are not [[absolutely continuous]], that is, <math>W_t</math> cannot be representated as an integral over a function <math>\xi</math>.

The mathematical formalization of the above defines a Gaussian white noise <math>G</math> (with Lebesgue intensity) as an [[isometry]] from the space of square-integrable functions <math>L^2(\R,\mathcal B(\R))</math> to the space of centered Gaussian random variables, that is, for <math>f,g\in L^2(\R)</math> the evaluation <math>G(f)</math> is a Gaussian random variable and

<math display="block">\begin{align}
&\operatorname E[G(f)]=0,\\
&\operatorname E[G(f),G(g)]=\langle f,g\rangle_{L^2(\R)}.
\end{align}</math>

Such a function <math>G</math> indeed exists. Intuitively (and again informally), the Gaussian white noise can be thought of as <math>G(f)=\langle\xi,f\rangle_{L^2(\R)}</math>, which means it is testing <math>\xi</math> against test functions <math>f</math> in the spirit of [[Distribution (mathematical analysis)|distribution theory]]. Using the linearity of <math>\langle\cdot,f\rangle</math> and the properties of <math>\xi</math> yields the properties of <math>G</math>.

This allows to define a ''pre-Brownian motion'' as

<math display="block">\tilde W_t:= G(1_{[0,t]}),\quad t\geq0.</math>

Pre-Brownian motions do not necessarily have continuous paths, but by [[Kolmogorov continuity theorem|Kolmogorov's continuity criterion]], there exists a [[Stochastic process#Modification|modification]] of <math>\tilde W</math> that does. Therefore, the Wiener process <math>W</math> can be defined as a pre-Brownian motion that has continuous paths.<ref name=":1" />

=== Donsker's theorem: Wiener process as a limit of a random walk ===
The Wiener process can be constructed as the [[scaling limit]] of a [[random walk]], or other discrete-time stochastic processes with stationary independent increments. This is known as [[Donsker's theorem]]. Like the random walk, the Wiener process is recurrent in one or two dimensions (meaning that it returns almost surely to any fixed [[neighborhood (mathematics)|neighborhood]] of the origin infinitely often) whereas it is not recurrent in dimensions three and higher (where a multidimensional Wiener process is a process such that its coordinates are independent Wiener processes).<ref>{{cite web |title= Pólya's Random Walk Constants |website= Wolfram Mathworld| url = https://mathworld.wolfram.com/PolyasRandomWalkConstants.html}}</ref> 

Let <math display="inline">\xi_1, \xi_2, \ldots</math> be [[Independent and identically distributed random variables|i.i.d.]] random variables with mean 0 and variance 1. For each {{mvar|n}}, define the constant interpolation of the [[random walk]] process

<math display="block">W_n(t)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}\sum\limits_{1\leq k\leq\lfloor nt\rfloor}\xi_k, \qquad t \in [0,1].</math>

This is a random step function. Increments of {{math|''W<sub>n</sub>''}} are independent because the <math display="inline">\xi_k</math> are independent. For large {{mvar|n}}, <math display="inline">W_n(t)-W_n(s)</math> is close to <math display="inline">N(0,t-s)</math> by the central limit theorem. [[Donsker's theorem]] asserts that as <math display="inline">n \to \infty</math>, {{math|''W<sub>n</sub>''}} approaches a Wiener process.

This characterization explains mathematically the ubiquity of Brownian motion in natural phenomena.<ref>{{cite web |last=Lalley |first=Steven |year=2001 |title=Mathematical Finance 345 Lecture 5: Brownian Motion |url=https://galton.uchicago.edu/~lalley/Courses/345/BrownianMotion.pdf |publisher=University of Chicago |access-date=2026-03-06}}</ref>

== Properties of a one-dimensional Wiener process ==
[[Image:Wiener-process-5traces.svg|thumb|upright=1.5|Five sampled processes, with expected standard deviation in gray]]

=== Basic properties ===

* Brownian motion is a centered [[Gaussian process]]. In particular, for <math>t>0</math>, <math>W_t = W_t-W_0 \sim N(0,t)</math>, that is, the [[probability density function]] of <math>W_t</math> is
<math display="block">f_{W_t}(x) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2 \pi t}} e^{-x^2/(2t)}.</math>
* The [[covariance function|covariance]] between <math>W_t</math> and <math>W_s</math> (<math display="inline">s \leq t</math>) is<ref name=":1" /><math display="block">\operatorname{cov}(W_s, W_t) = \operatorname E[W_sW_t] = s.</math> In particular, the [[variance]] is <math>\operatorname{Var}(W_t) = t.</math>

* The [[correlation function|correlation]] between <math>W_t</math> and <math>W_s</math> (<math display="inline">s \leq t</math>) is
<math display="block">\operatorname{corr}(W_s,W_t) = \frac{\operatorname{cov}(W_s,W_t)}{\sigma_{W_s} \sigma_{W_t}} = \frac{s}{\sqrt{st}} = \sqrt{\frac{s}{t}}.</math>
* A useful decomposition for proving martingale properties, also called ''Brownian increment decomposition'', is
<math display="block">W_t = W_s + (W_t - W_s),\; s \le t.</math>
* Brownian motion is a [[Lévy process]]. In particular, it has [[Stationary increments|stationary]] and [[independent increments]].
* Brownian motion is a continuous [[Martingale (probability theory)|martingale]].<ref name=":1" />
* Brownian motion has the [[Markov property|strong Markov property]].<ref name=":3" />

=== Covariance and correlation ===
The [[covariance function|covariance]] and [[correlation function|correlation]] between <math>W_t</math> and <math>W_s</math> follow from the definition that non-overlapping increments are independent, of which only the property that they are uncorrelated is used.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Stark |first1=Henry |last2=Woods |first2=John |title=Probability and Random Processes with Applications to Signal Processing |edition=3rd |publisher=Prentice Hall |location=New Jersey |year=2002 |isbn=0-13-020071-9 }}</ref> Suppose that <math display="inline">t_1\leq t_2</math>.

<math display="block">\operatorname{cov}(W_{t_1}, W_{t_2}) = \operatorname{E}\left[(W_{t_1}-\operatorname{E}[W_{t_1}]) \cdot (W_{t_2}-\operatorname{E}[W_{t_2}])\right] = \operatorname{E}\left[W_{t_1} \cdot W_{t_2} \right].</math>

Substituting
<math display="block"> W_{t_2} = ( W_{t_2} - W_{t_1} ) + W_{t_1} </math>
we arrive at:
<math display="block">\begin{align}
\operatorname{E}[W_{t_1} \cdot W_{t_2}] & = \operatorname{E}\left[W_{t_1} \cdot ((W_{t_2} - W_{t_1})+ W_{t_1}) \right] \\
& = \operatorname{E}\left[W_{t_1} \cdot (W_{t_2} - W_{t_1} )\right] + \operatorname{E}\left[ W_{t_1}^2 \right].
\end{align}</math>

Since <math display="inline"> W_{t_1}=W_{t_1} - W_{t_0} </math> and <math display="inline"> W_{t_2} - W_{t_1} </math> are independent,
<math display="block"> \operatorname{E}\left [W_{t_1} \cdot (W_{t_2} - W_{t_1} ) \right ] = \operatorname{E}[W_{t_1}] \cdot \operatorname{E}[W_{t_2} - W_{t_1}] = 0.</math>

Thus
<math display="block">\operatorname{cov}(W_{t_1}, W_{t_2}) = \operatorname{E} \left [W_{t_1}^2 \right ] = t_1.</math>

A corollary useful for simulation is that we can write, for {{math|''t''<sub>1</sub> < ''t''<sub>2</sub>}}:
<math display="block">W_{t_2} = W_{t_1}+\sqrt{t_2-t_1}\cdot Z</math>
where {{mvar|Z}} is an independent standard normal variable.

=== Infinitesimal generator ===
The [[Infinitesimal generator (stochastic processes)|infinitesimal generator]] of Brownian motion is given by<ref name=":2" />

<math display="block">Af(x) = \lim_{t\to 0}\frac{\operatorname E[f(W_t+x)]-f(x)}{t} = \frac{1}{2} f''(x), \quad x\in\R,</math>

for all <math>f\in C^2(\R)</math> that vanish at infinity. This is an almost direct consequence of [[Itô's lemma|Itô's formula]].

=== Running maximum ===
The joint distribution of the running maximum

<math display="block"> M_t = \max_{0 \leq s \leq t} W_s </math>

and {{math|''W<sub>t</sub>''}} is<ref name=":1" />

<math display="block"> f_{M_t,W_t}(m,w) = \frac{2(2m - w)}{t\sqrt{2 \pi t}} e^{-\frac{(2m-w)^2}{2t}}, \qquad m \ge 0, w \leq m.</math>

To get the unconditional distribution of <math display="inline">f_{M_t}</math>, integrate over {{math|−∞ < ''w'' ≤ ''m''}}:
<math display="block">\begin{align}
f_{M_t}(m) & = \int_{-\infty}^m f_{M_t,W_t}(m,w)\,dw = \int_{-\infty}^m \frac{2(2m - w)}{t\sqrt{2 \pi t}} e^{-\frac{(2m-w)^2}{2t}} \,dw \\[5pt]
& = \sqrt{\frac{2}{\pi t}}e^{-\frac{m^2}{2t}}, \qquad m \ge 0,
\end{align}</math>

the probability density function of a [[Half-normal distribution]]. The expectation<ref>{{cite book|last=Shreve|first=Steven E.| title=Stochastic Calculus for Finance II: Continuous-Time Models|year=2008|publisher=Springer| isbn=978-0-387-40101-0| pages=114}}</ref> is
<math display="block"> \operatorname{E}[M_t] = \int_0^\infty m f_{M_t}(m)\,dm  = \int_0^\infty m \sqrt{\frac{2}{\pi t}}e^{-\frac{m^2}{2t}}\,dm = \sqrt{\frac{2t}{\pi}} </math>

If at time {{mvar|t}} the Wiener process has a known value <math display="inline">W_{t}</math>, it is possible to calculate the conditional probability distribution of the maximum in interval <math display="inline">[0, t]</math> (cf. [[Probability distribution of extreme points of a Wiener stochastic process]]). The  [[cumulative probability distribution function]] of the maximum value, [[Conditional probability|conditioned]] by the known value <math display="inline">W_t</math>, is:
<math display="block">\, F_{M_{W_t}} (m)  = \Pr \left( M_{W_t} = \max_{0 \leq s \leq t} W_s \leq m \mid  W_t \right) = \ 1 -\ e^{-2\frac{m(m - W_t)}{t}}\ \, , \,\ \   m > \max(0,W_t)</math>

=== Arcsine laws ===
{{Main|Arcsine laws (Wiener process)}}
There are multiple (random) quantities <math>T</math> related to Brownian motion that follow the [[arcsine distribution]]:

<math display="block">\Pr(T\leq t)=\frac{2}{\pi}\arcsin(\sqrt{t}),\quad t\in[0,1].</math>

These statements are referred to as the [[Arcsine laws (Wiener process)|arcsine laws]] of Brownian motion.

==== First arcsine law ====
The amount of time Brownian motion is positive, that is,

<math display="block">T=\int_0^1 1_{\{W_t>0\}}\mathrm d t ,</math>

is arcsine-distributed.

==== Second arcsine law ====
The last time Brownian motion hits zero in the time interval <math>[0,1]</math>, that is,

<math display="block">T=\sup\{t\leq 1: W_t=0\},</math>

is arcsine-distributed.<ref name=":3" />

==== Third arcsine law ====
The time at which Brownian motion attains its maximum on <math>[0,1]</math>, that is,

<math display="block">T=\inf\left\{t\leq 1: W_t=\max_{s\in[0,1]}W_s\right\},</math>

is arcsine-distributed.<ref name=":1" />

=== Self-similarity ===
[[File:Wiener process animated.gif|thumb|500px|A demonstration of Brownian scaling, showing <math display=inline>V_t = (1/\sqrt c) W_{ct}</math> for decreasing {{mvar|c}}. Note that the average features of the function do not change while zooming in, and note that it zooms in quadratically faster horizontally than vertically. ]]

==== Brownian scaling ====
For every {{math|''c'' > 0}} the process <math display=inline> V_t = (1 / \sqrt c) W_{ct} </math> is another Wiener process.

==== Time reversal ====
The process <math display=inline> V_t = W_{1-t} - W_{1} </math> for {{math|0 ≤ ''t'' ≤ 1}} is distributed like {{math|''W<sub>t</sub>''}} for {{math|0 ≤ ''t'' ≤ 1}}.

==== Time inversion ====
The process <math display=inline> V_t = t W_{1/t} </math> is another Wiener process.

==== Projective invariance ====
Consider a Wiener process <math display=inline>W(t)</math>, <math display=inline>t\in\mathbb R</math>, conditioned so that <math display=inline>\lim_{t\to\pm\infty}tW(t)=0</math> (which holds almost surely) and as usual <math display=inline>W(0)=0</math>.  Then the following are all Wiener processes:<ref>{{cite journal |title=On pathwise projective invariance of Brownian motion |first=Shigeo |last=Takenaka |journal=Proceedings of the Japan Academy, Series A, Mathematical Sciences |volume=64 |issue=2 |year=1988 |pages=41–44 |doi=10.3792/pjaa.64.41}}</ref>
<math display="block">
\begin{array}{rcl}
W_{1,s}(t) &=& W(t+s)-W(s), \quad s\in\mathbb R\\
W_{2,\sigma}(t) &=& \sigma^{-1/2}W(\sigma t),\quad \sigma > 0\\
W_3(t) &=& tW(-1/t).
\end{array}
</math>
Thus the Wiener process is invariant under the projective group [[PSL(2,R)]], being invariant under the generators of the group.  The action of an element <math display=inline>g = \begin{bmatrix}a&b\\c&d\end{bmatrix}</math> is
<math display="block">W_g(t) = (ct+d)W\left(\frac{at+b}{ct+d}\right) - ctW\left(\frac{a}{c}\right) - dW\left(\frac{b}{d}\right),</math>
which defines a [[group action]], in the sense that <math display=inline>(W_g)_h = W_{gh}.</math>

==== Conformal invariance in two dimensions ====
Let <math display="inline">W</math> be a two-dimensional Wiener process, regarded as a complex-valued process with <math display="inline">W_0=0\in\mathbb C</math>.  Let <math display=inline>D\subset\mathbb C</math> be an open set containing 0, and <math display=inline>\tau_D</math> be associated Markov time:
<math display="block">\tau_D = \inf \{ t\ge 0 |W_t \not\in D\}.</math>
If <math display=inline>f:D\to \mathbb C</math> is a [[holomorphic function]] which is not constant, such that <math display=inline>f(0)=0</math>, then <math display=inline>f(W_t)</math> is a time-changed Wiener process in <math display=inline>f(D)</math>.<ref>{{cite book |first=Greg |last=Lawler |title=Conformally invariant processes in the plane |publisher=American Mathematical Society |year=2005 |isbn=978-0821836774}}</ref> More precisely, the process <math display="inline">Y</math> is Wiener in {{mvar|D}} with the Markov time <math display="inline">S</math>, where
<math display="block">Y_t = f(W_{\sigma(t)})</math>
<math display="block">S(t) = \int_0^t|f'(W_s)|^2\,ds</math>
<math display="block">\sigma(t) = S^{-1}(t):\quad t = \int_0^{\sigma(t)}|f'(W_s)|^2\,ds.</math>

=== Stopping times ===

==== Hitting time of level sets ====
The first hitting time <math>T_a</math> of the Wiener process of some value <math>a>0</math>, that is,

<math display="block">T_a=\inf\{t\geq 0: W_t=a\},</math>

is [[Lévy distribution|Lévy-distributed]], which means it has the Lebesgue density

<math display="block">f(t)=\frac{a}{\sqrt{2\pi t^3}}\exp\left(-\frac{a^2}{2t}\right)1_{[0,\infty)}(t), \quad t\in\R.</math>

In particular, <math>\operatorname E[T_a]=\infty</math>. Moreover, <math>T_a</math> has the same distribution as <math>a^2/W_1^2</math>.<ref name=":1" />

==== Exit time of intervals ====
Let <math>\tau_a</math> be the first exit time of the interval <math>[-a,a]</math>. Its expectation equals

<math display="block">\operatorname E[\tau_a]=a^2,</math>

and its [[Laplace transform]] is<ref name=":1" />

<math display="block">\operatorname E[e^{-t\tau_a}] = \frac{1}{\cosh(a\sqrt{2t})}, \quad t\geq 0.</math>

==== Hitting times of two level sets ====
Let <math>a<0<b</math> and <math>T_c=\inf\{t\geq 0: W_t=c\}</math> be the first hitting time of a value <math>c\in\R</math>. Then,<ref name=":1" />

<math display="block">\operatorname P(T_a<T_b) = \frac{b}{b-a},\qquad \operatorname P(T_b<T_a) = -\frac{a}{b-a}.</math>

=== A class of Brownian martingales ===
If a [[polynomial]] {{math|''p''(''x'', ''t'')}} satisfies the [[partial differential equation]]
<math display="block">\left( \frac{\partial}{\partial t} + \frac{1}{2} \frac{\partial^2}{\partial x^2} \right) p(x,t) = 0 </math>
then the stochastic process
<math display="block"> M_t = p ( W_t, t )</math>
is a [[martingale (probability theory)|martingale]].

'''Example:''' <math display=inline> W_t^2 - t </math> is a martingale, which shows that the [[quadratic variation]] of {{mvar|W}} on {{closed-closed|0, ''t''}} is equal to {{mvar|t}}. It follows that the expected [[first exit time|time of first exit]] of {{mvar|W}} from (−''c'', ''c'') is equal to {{math|''c''<sup>2</sup>}}.

More generally, for every polynomial {{math|''p''(''x'', ''t'')}} the following stochastic process is a martingale:
<math display="block"> M_t = p ( W_t, t ) - \int_0^t a(W_s,s) \, \mathrm{d}s, </math>
where {{mvar|a}} is the polynomial
<math display="block"> a(x,t) = \left( \frac{\partial}{\partial t} + \frac 1 2 \frac{\partial^2}{\partial x^2} \right) p(x,t). </math>

'''Example:''' <math display=inline> p(x,t) = \left(x^2 - t\right)^2, </math> <math display=inline> a(x,t) = 4x^2; </math> the process
<math display="block"> \left(W_t^2 - t\right)^2 - 4 \int_0^t W_s^2 \, \mathrm{d}s </math>
is a martingale, which shows that the quadratic variation of the martingale <math display=inline> W_t^2 - t </math> on [0, ''t''] is equal to
<math display="block"> 4 \int_0^t W_s^2 \, \mathrm{d}s.</math>

About functions {{math|''p''(''xa'', ''t'')}} more general than polynomials, see [[Local martingale#Martingales via local martingales|local martingales]].

=== Properties of sample paths ===
The set of all functions {{mvar|w}} with the following properties has probability one under the Wiener measure. That is, a path (sample function) of the Wiener process has all these properties almost surely:

==== Qualitative properties ====
* For every ε > 0, the function {{mvar|w}} takes both (strictly) positive and (strictly) negative values on (0, ε).<ref name=":1">{{cite book |last=Le Gall |first=Jean-François |year=2016 |title=Brownian Motion, Martingales, and Stochastic Calculus |publisher=[[Springer Science+Business Media|Springer]] |series=Graduate Texts in Mathematics |volume=274 |isbn=978-3-319-31088-6 |page=|pages=11-19,20, 30, 32, 37, 39, 50, 51, 62, 63, 119, 121, 127, 155-161}}</ref>
* The function {{mvar|w}} is continuous everywhere, but nowhere differentiable (like the [[Weierstrass function]]).<ref name=":0" />
* For any <math display=inline>\epsilon > 0</math>, <math display="inline">w</math> is nowhere <math display="inline">(\tfrac 1 2 + \epsilon)</math>-[[Hölder continuous]],<ref name=":3">{{Cite book |last=Klenke |first=Achim |title=Probability Theory |publisher=[[Springer Science+Business Media|Springer]] |year=2020 |isbn=978-3-030-56401-8 |edition=3rd |pages=524, 526, 529, 531}}</ref> but it is locally <math display="inline">(\tfrac 1 2 - \epsilon)</math>-Hölder continuous.<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Mörters |first1=Peter |title=Brownian motion |last2=Peres |first2=Yuval |last3=Schramm |first3=Oded |last4=Werner |first4=Wendelin |date=2010 |publisher=Cambridge University Press |isbn=978-0-521-76018-8 |series=Cambridge series in statistical and probabilistic mathematics |location=Cambridge |pages=18}}</ref>
* Points of [[Maxima and minima|local maximum]] of the function {{mvar|w}} are a dense countable set;<ref name=":0" /> the maximum values are pairwise different; each local maximum is sharp in the following sense: if {{mvar|w}} has a local maximum at {{mvar|t}} then <math display="block">\lim_{s \to t} \frac{|w(s)-w(t)|}{|s-t|} =\infty.</math> The same holds for local minima.
* The function {{mvar|w}} has no points of local increase, that is, no {{math|''t'' > 0}} satisfies the following for some ε in (0, ''t''): first, {{math|''w''(''s'') ≤ ''w''(''t'')}} for all {{mvar|s}} in (''t'' − ε, ''t''), and second, {{math|''w''(''s'') ≥ ''w''(''t'')}} for all {{mvar|s}} in (''t'', ''t'' + ε). (Local increase is a weaker condition than that {{mvar|w}} is increasing on (''t'' − ''ε'', ''t'' + ''ε'').) The same holds for local decrease.<ref name=":0" />
* The function {{mvar|w}} is of [[bounded variation|unbounded variation]] on every interval.<ref name=":1" />
* The [[quadratic variation]] of {{mvar|w}} over [0,''t''] is {{mvar|t}}. 
* The set <math>\{t\geq 0: w(t)=0\}</math> of [[root of a function|Zeros]] of the function {{mvar|w}} is [[perfect set|perfect]] (closed and contains no isolated points), is [[nowhere dense set|nowhere dense]], has Lebesgue measure 0 and has [[Hausdorff dimension]] 1/2 (therefore, is uncountable).

While it is not true that a path of Brownian motion is almost surely nowhere <math display="inline">\tfrac 1 2</math>-Hölder continuous, for a fixed <math>t\geq 0</math>, it can be asserted that a path is almost surely not <math display="inline">\tfrac 1 2</math>-Hölder continuous in <math>t</math>.<ref name=":1" />

==== Quantitative properties ====

===== [[Law of the iterated logarithm]] =====
<math display="block"> \limsup_{t\to+\infty} \frac{ |w(t)| }{ \sqrt{ 2t \log\log t } } = 1, \quad \text{almost surely}. </math>

===== [[Modulus of continuity]] =====
Local modulus of continuity:
<math display="block"> \limsup_{\varepsilon \to 0+} \frac{ |w(\varepsilon)| }{ \sqrt{ 2\varepsilon \log\log(1/\varepsilon) } } = 1, \qquad \text{almost surely}. </math>

[[Lévy's modulus of continuity theorem|Global modulus of continuity]] (Lévy):
<math display="block"> \limsup_{\varepsilon\to0+} \sup_{0\le s<t\le 1, t-s\le\varepsilon}\frac{|w(s)-w(t)|}{\sqrt{ 2\varepsilon \log(1/\varepsilon)}} = 1, \qquad \text{almost surely}. </math>

===== [[Dimension doubling theorem]] =====
The dimension doubling theorems say that the [[Hausdorff dimension]] of a set under a Brownian motion doubles almost surely.

==== Local time ====
The image of the [[Lebesgue measure]] on [0, ''t''] under the map {{mvar|w}} (the [[pushforward measure]]) has a density {{math|''L''<sub>''t''</sub>}}.  Thus,
<math display="block"> \int_0^t f(w(s)) \, \mathrm{d}s = \int_{-\infty}^{+\infty} f(x) L_t(x) \, \mathrm{d}x </math>
for a wide class of functions {{mvar|f}} (namely: all continuous functions; all locally integrable functions; all non-negative measurable functions). The density {{math|''L<sub>t</sub>''}} is (more exactly, can and will be chosen to be) continuous. The number {{math|''L<sub>t</sub>''(''x'')}} is called the [[local time (mathematics)|local time]] at {{mvar|x}} of {{mvar|w}} on [0, ''t'']. It is strictly positive for all {{mvar|x}} of the interval (''a'', ''b'') where ''a'' and ''b'' are the least and the greatest value of {{mvar|w}} on [0, ''t''], respectively. (For {{mvar|x}} outside this interval the local time evidently vanishes.) Treated as a function of two variables {{mvar|x}} and {{mvar|t}}, the local time is still continuous. Treated as a function of {{mvar|t}} (while {{mvar|x}} is fixed), the local time is a [[singular function]] corresponding to a [[atom (measure theory)|nonatomic]] measure on the set of zeros of {{mvar|w}}.

These continuity properties are fairly non-trivial. Consider that the local time can also be defined (as the density of the pushforward measure) for a smooth function. Then, however,  the density is discontinuous, unless the given function is monotone. In other words, there is a conflict between good behavior of a function and good behavior of its local time. In this sense, the continuity of the local time of the Wiener process is another manifestation of non-smoothness of the trajectory.

=== Information rate ===
The [[information rate]] of the Wiener process with respect to the squared error distance, i.e. its quadratic [[rate-distortion function]], is given by <ref>{{cite journal |last=Berger |first=Toby |year=1970 |title=Information rates of Wiener processes |journal=IEEE Transactions on Information Theory |volume=16 |issue=2 |pages=134–139 |doi=10.1109/TIT.1970.1054423}}</ref>
<math display="block">R(D) = \frac{2}{\pi^2 D \ln 2} \approx 0.29D^{-1}.</math>
Therefore, it is impossible to encode <math display=inline>\{w_t \}_{t \in [0,T]}</math> using a [[binary code]] of less than <math display=inline>T R(D)</math> [[bit]]s and recover it with expected mean squared error less than {{mvar|D}}. On the other hand, for any <math display=inline> \varepsilon>0</math>, there exists {{mvar|T}} large enough and a [[binary code]] of no more than <math display=inline>2^{TR(D)}</math> distinct elements such that the expected [[mean squared error]] in recovering <math display=inline>\{w_t \}_{t \in [0,T]}</math> from this code is at most <math display=inline>D - \varepsilon</math>.

In many cases, it is impossible to [[binary code|encode]] the Wiener process without [[Sampling (signal processing)|sampling]] it first. When the Wiener process is sampled at intervals <math display=inline>T_s</math> before applying a binary code to represent these samples, the optimal trade-off between [[code rate]] <math display=inline>R(T_s,D)</math> and expected [[mean square error]] {{mvar|D}} (in estimating the continuous-time Wiener process) follows the parametric representation <ref>{{cite journal |last1=Kipnis |first1=Alon |last2=Goldsmith |first2=Andrea J. |last3=Eldar |first3=Yonina C. |year=2019 |title=The distortion-rate function of sampled Wiener processes |journal=IEEE Transactions on Information Theory |volume=65 |issue=1 |pages=482–499 |doi=10.1109/TIT.2018.2869911}}</ref>
<math display="block"> R(T_s,D_\theta) =  \frac{T_s}{2} \int_0^1 \log_2^+\left[\frac{S(\varphi)- \frac{1}{6}}{\theta}\right] d\varphi, </math>
<math display="block"> D_\theta =  \frac{T_s}{6} + T_s\int_0^1 \min\left\{S(\varphi)-\frac{1}{6},\theta \right\} d\varphi, </math>
where <math display=inline>S(\varphi) = (2 \sin(\pi \varphi /2))^{-2}</math> and <math display=inline>\log^+[x] = \max\{0,\log(x)\}</math>. In particular, <math display=inline>T_s/6</math> is the mean squared error associated only with the sampling operation (without encoding).

== {{mvar|d}}-dimensional Wiener process ==
A Wiener process can be straighforwardly extended to higher dimensions <math>d\geq 2</math> as follows.

=== Definition ===
A process <math>W=(W^1,\dots,W^d)</math> is a <math>d</math>-dimensional Wiener process, if <math>W^1,\dots,W^d</math> are independent one-dimensional Wiener processes.<ref name=":1" />

=== Lévy characterization ===
Let <math>W=(W^1,\dots,W^d)</math> be an adapted stochastic process. The following are equivalent:<ref name=":1" />

* <math>W</math> is a <math>d</math>-dimensional Wiener process.
* <math>W^1,\dots,W^d</math> are continuous local martingales and for <math>i,j\in\{1,\dots,d\}</math>, the covariation fulfills <math>\langle W^i,W^j \rangle_t=\delta_{ij}t</math> for all <math>t\geq 0</math>, where <math>\delta_{ij}</math> is the [[Kronecker delta]].

=== Generator representation ===
The Wiener process can also be defined as the unique continuous Markov process starting in zero almost surely and whose generator is <math>A=\frac{1}{2}\Delta</math> with domain <math>\mathrm{Dom}(A)=\{f\in C^2(\R^d): f,\partial_{ij}^2 f \in C_0(\R^d)\}</math>, where <math>C_0(\R^d)</math> denotes the space of continuous functions vanishing at infinity.

In fact, given the above generator <math>A</math>, there exist a unique Feller semigroup <math>(P_t)_{t\geq 0}</math>, that is, <math>P_t</math> is a [[Markov kernel]] with

# <math>\forall x\in\R^d: P_0(x,\cdot)=\delta_x</math>, the [[Dirac measure]],
# <math>\forall s,t\geq 0,\,A\in\mathcal B(\R^d): P_{t+s}(x,A)=\int_{\R^d}P_t(y,A)P_s(x,\mathrm{d}y)</math>,
# <math>\forall f\in C_0(\R^d): P_tf\equiv \int_{\R^d} f(y) P_t(\cdot,\mathrm{d}y)\in C_0(\R^d)</math>,
# <math>\forall f\in C_0(\R^d): \lim_{t\to0}\lVert P_tf-f\rVert_{L^\infty(\R^d)}=0</math>.


such that

<math display="block">Af=\lim_{t\to0}\frac{P_tf-f}{t}, \qquad f\in\mathrm{Dom}(A).</math>

In this case, for <math>f\in\mathrm{Dom}(A)</math>, the correspondence is precisely

<math display="block">P_tf(x)=e^{At}f(x) = \int_{\R^d}\frac{1}{(2\pi t)^{d/2}}\exp\left(-\frac{\lVert x-y\rVert^2}{2t} \right)f(y)\mathrm{d}y, \quad x\in\R^d.</math>

At the same time, there exist a unique Markov process <math>W</math> on <math>(\R^{[0,\infty)},\mathcal B(\R)^{\otimes[0,\infty)})</math> starting in zero such that

<math display="block">\mathrm{Pr}(W_t+x\in\cdot)=P_t(x,\cdot), \qquad \forall t\geq 0,\, x\in\R^d,</math>

that is, the transition probabilities of <math>W_t+x</math> are given by <math>P_t(x,\cdot)</math>. Finally, by [[Kolmogorov continuity theorem|Kolmorov's continuity criterion]], there exists a [[Stochastic process#Modification|modification]] of <math>W</math> with continuous paths, which is the Wiener process.<ref name=":1" />

== Properties of a {{mvar|d}}-dimensional Wiener process ==

=== Path properties ===
The following path properties hold almost surely (some of them follow directly from those of the one-dimensional Wiener process):

* The paths are everywhere continuous, but nowhere differentiable.
* For any <math display="inline">\epsilon > 0</math>, the paths are nowhere <math display="inline">(\tfrac 1 2 + \epsilon)</math>-[[Hölder continuous]], but locally <math display="inline">(\tfrac 1 2 - \epsilon)</math>-Hölder continuous.
* For <math>d=2</math>, the Wiener process is recurrent, that is, for every Borel set <math>A</math>, if the first hitting time <math>\inf\{t>0:W_t\in A\}</math> is not almost surely infinite, then <math>\operatorname{Pr}(W_t\in A\text{ for infinitely many }t>0)=1</math>. In particular, the Wiener process returns arbitrarily close to the origin infinitely often almost surely.<ref name=":4">{{Cite book |last=Chung |first=Kai Lai |title=Markov Processes, Brownian Motion, and Time Symmetry |last2=Walsh |first2=John B. |publisher=[[Springer Science+Business Media|Springer]] |year=2005 |isbn=978-0387-22026-0 |edition=2nd |pages=122-129, 145, 166, 169, 181}}</ref>
* For <math>d\geq 3</math>, every compact set <math>K</math> is transient, that is, the last hitting time <math>\sup\{t\geq0:W_t\in K\}</math> is almost surely finite. In particular, the Wiener process returns in a neighborhood of the origin only finitely many times almost surely.<ref name=":4" />

=== Infinitesimal generator ===
Similarly to the one-dimensional case, the [[Infinitesimal generator (stochastic processes)|infinitesimal generator]] of Brownian motion is given by<ref name=":2" />

<math display="block">Af(x) = \lim_{t\to 0}\frac{\operatorname E[f(W_t+x)]-f(x)}{t} = \frac{1}{2} \Delta f(x), \quad x\in\R^d,</math>

where <math>\Delta</math> is the [[Laplace operator]], for all <math>f\in C^2(\R^d)</math> that vanish at infinity.

=== Harmonic measure on the sphere ===
The [[Harmonic measure#The harmonic measure of a diffusion|harmonic measure]] of Brownian motion on the sphere <math>\mathbb{S}_{d-1}</math>, that is, the distribution of <math>W_\tau</math>, where <math>\tau=\inf\{t\geq 0: W_t\in \mathbb{S}_{d-1}\}</math> is the first hitting time of the unit sphere, when the process is started in <math>x\in B_1(0)</math>, is

<math display="block">\mu^x(A)\equiv\operatorname{Pr}(W_\tau+x\in A)=\int_{\mathbb{S}_{d-1}}1_A(y) q(x,y)\mathrm{d}\sigma(y), \qquad A\in\mathcal B(\R^d),</math>

where <math>\sigma</math> is the surface measure and

<math display="block">q(x,y)=\frac{1}{\sigma(\mathbb{S}_{d-1})}\frac{1-\lVert x\rVert^2}{\lVert x-y\rVert^d}, \quad x\in B_1(0),\,y\in\mathbb{S}_{d-1},</math>

is the [[Poisson kernel]] for the unit ball.<ref name=":4" />

=== Occupation time formula ===
Let <math>D\subset\R^d</math> be an open, bounded set and <math>\tau_D^x=\inf\{t\geq 0: W_t+x\in\partial D\}</math> be the first exit time of Brownian motion, when started in <math>x\in D</math>. Then, the occupation time of a set <math>A\in\mathcal B(\R^d)</math> is given by

<math display="block">\operatorname E\left[\int_0^{\tau_D^x}1_A(W_t+x)\mathrm d t \right] = \int_{\R^d} 1_A(y)G(x,y)\mathrm d y,</math>

where <math>G</math> is the [[Green's function|Green function]] of the Laplace operator for the domain <math>D</math>, that is, the (distributional) solution of the equation

<math display="block">\begin{align}
-\Delta G(x,\cdot) &= \delta_x, \quad\ \ \, \text{in } D \\
G(x,\cdot) &= 0, \qquad \text{on }\partial D
\end{align}</math>

where <math>\delta_x</math> is the [[Dirac measure]] in <math>x</math>. More generally, for a measurable function <math>f</math> that is either non-negative or integrable with respect to <math>G(x,\cdot)\mathrm d\lambda</math>, it holds<ref name=":4" />

<math display="block">\operatorname E\left[\int_0^{\tau_D^x} f(W_t+x)\mathrm d t \right] = \int_{\R^d} f(y)G(x,y)\mathrm d y.</math>

=== Representation of harmonic functions ===
Let <math>D\subset\R^d</math> be a bounded open set. Let <math>u</math> be [[Harmonic function|harmonic]] (<math>\Delta u=0</math>) in <math>D</math> and continuous in <math>\bar D</math>. Then,

<math display="block">u(x)=\operatorname E[u(W_{\tau_D^x}+x)], \quad x\in \bar D,</math>

where <math>\tau_D^x=\inf\{t\geq 0:W_t+x\in D^c\}</math> is the first exit time of the Wiener process from <math>D</math> when started in <math>x</math>.<ref name=":4" />

=== Stopping times ===

==== Moments of exit times ====
Let <math>D\subset\R^d</math> be a bounded open domain with smooth boundary and let <math>\tau_x=\inf\{t\geq 0:W_t+x\in D^c\} </math>. Then, for <math>k\in\N</math>, the function

<math display="block">u_k(x) = \operatorname E[\tau_x^k], \quad x\in \bar D, </math>

is the solution to the recursive differential equation

<math display="block">\begin{cases}
&\frac{1}{2}\Delta u_1 +1=0, &k=1 \\
&\frac{1}{2}\Delta u_k+ku_{k-1}=0, &k\geq 2
\end{cases}\quad\text{ on }D</math>

with the boundary condition <math>u_k=0</math> on <math>\partial D</math>.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Kinateder |first=K.K.J. |last2=McDonald |first2=P. |last3=Miller |first3=D. |date=1998 |title=Exit time moments, boundary value problems, and the geometry of domains in Euclidean space |url=https://doi.org/10.1007/s004400050174 |journal=Probability Theory and Related Fields |volume=111 |pages=469–487}}</ref> In particular, when <math>D</math> is the ball with radius <math>R</math>, then

<math display="block">\operatorname E[\tau_x]=\frac{R^2-\lVert x\rVert^2}{d}.</math>

==== Distribution of exit time from a ball ====
Let <math>\tau_R=\inf\{t\geq 0:W_t\notin B_R\} </math> be the first exit time of Brownian motion from the ball with radius <math>R</math> and centered in the origin. Then<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Ciesielski |first=Z. |last2=Taylor |first2=S.J. |date=1962 |title=First Passage times and Sojourn Times for Brownian Motion in Space and the Exact Hausdorff Measure of the Sample Path |journal=Transactions of the American Mathematical Society |volume=103 |issue=3 |pages=434-450}}</ref>

<math display="block">\operatorname{Pr}(\tau_R>t) = \sum_{k=1}^\infty c_{k,d}\exp\left(-\frac{q_{k,d}^2}{2R^2}t\right),</math>

where <math>q_{1,d}<q_{2,d}<\dots </math> are the positive roots of the [[Bessel function]] <math>J_{d/2-1}</math> and

<math display="block">c_{k,d} = \frac{q_{k,d}^{d/2-2}}{2^{d/2-2}\Gamma(d/2)J_{d/2}(q_{k,d})}</math>

with the [[Gamma function]] <math>\Gamma</math>. In particular, <math>\tau_R</math> has exponential tails.

== Wiener process on Riemannian manifolds ==
[[File:BMonSphere.jpg|thumb|The [[Infinitesimal generator (stochastic processes)|generator]] of Brownian motion on [[Riemannian manifold]]s is {{frac|1|2}} times the [[Laplace–Beltrami operator]]. The image above shows Brownian motion on the surface of a 2-sphere.]]
The Wiener process can be generalized in such a way that it evolves only on a Riemannian manifold <math>M\subset\R^d</math> such as a sphere. This requires the [[Orthogonal projection|orthogonal projections]] <math>P(x)</math> onto the [[tangent space]] <math>T_xM</math> for all <math>x\in M</math>. With this definition, the Wiener process <math>X</math> on <math>M</math> is defined as the solution to the Stratonovich equation
<math display="block">\mathrm dX_t^i =\sum_{j=1}^dP(x)_{ij}\circ\mathrm d W_t^j, \qquad X_0\in M,</math>
where <math>W=(W^1,\dots,W^d)</math> is a <math>d</math>-dimensional standard Wiener process. It can be shown that <math>X</math> indeed evolves in <math>M</math> (which would not be case the solution to the same equation with the Stratonovich replaced by the Itô integral). Moreover, the [[Infinitesimal generator (stochastic processes)|infinitesimal generator]] of <math>X</math> is one-half the [[Laplace–Beltrami operator]], which is a generalization of the Laplace operator for Riemannian manifolds.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Rogers |first=L.C.G. |title=Diffusion, Markov Processes, and Martingales |last2=Williams |first2=David |publisher=Cambridge University Press |year=2000 |isbn=0521775930 |edition=2nd |volume=2 |pages=183}}</ref><ref name=":5">{{Cite book |last=Hsu |first=Elton P. |title=Stochastic Analysis on Manifolds |publisher=American Mathematical Society |year=2002 |isbn=9780821883884 |pages=78-83}}</ref>

The special case of the unit sphere <math>\mathbb S_{d-1}</math> possesses the projection operator
<math display="block">P(x)y = y-\langle y,x\rangle x, \quad y\in\R^d,</math>
which leads to the Stroock representation of spherical Brownian motion<ref name=":5" />
<math display="block">X_t = X_0 + \int_0^t(\delta_{ij}-X_s^i X_s^j)\circ \mathrm dW_s^j.</math>

== Infinite dimensional Wiener process ==
The Wiener process can be generalized to a process taking values in an arbitrary [[Separable space|separable]] [[Hilbert space]] (which means it possesses an [[orthonormal basis]]), although some technical difficulties arise. The construction of a Hilbert space-valued Wiener process is the starting point for [[Stochastic partial differential equation|stochastic partial differential equations]], which are generalizations of [[Partial differential equation|partial differential equations]] driven by a Wiener process in time.

The definition of the Wiener process on a separable Hilbert space <math>(H,\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle)</math> requires the notion of a Gaussian random variable on <math>H</math>. Similarly to the <math>d</math>-dimensional case with <math>d>1</math>, a random variable <math>Z</math> with values in <math>(H,\mathcal B(H))</math> is Gaussian if for all <math>h\in H</math> the projection <math>\langle Z,h\rangle</math> is univariate Gaussian. One can show that the law of <math>Z</math> is uniquely determined by its mean <math>m\in H</math> and covariance operator <math>Q</math> (non-negative, [[Self-adjoint operator|symmetric]] and the series of [[Eigenvalues and eigenvectors|eigenvalues]] is summable) via<ref name=":6">{{Cite book |last=Liu |first=Wei |title=Stochastic Partial Differential Equations: An Introduction |last2=Röckner |first2=Michael |publisher=[[Springer Science+Business Media|Springer]] |year=2015 |isbn=978-3-319-22353-7 |pages=9,10,14,18,50}}</ref>

<math display="block">\begin{align}
&\operatorname E[\langle Z,h\rangle] = \langle m,h\rangle, \\
&\operatorname E[\langle Z-m,g\rangle\langle Z-m,h\rangle] = \langle g,Qh\rangle.
\end{align}</math>

In this case, one writes <math>Z\sim\mathcal N(m,Q)</math>.

The condition that the eigenvalues <math>(\lambda_k)_{k\in\N}</math> of <math>Q</math> fulfill

<math display="block">\sum_{k=1}^\infty |\lambda_k|<\infty</math>

is called ''trace-class'' and excludes, in particular, the identity operator from the definition.

=== ''Q''-Wiener process ===
Given a non-negative, symmetric, trace-class operator <math>Q</math>, a stochastic process <math>W^Q=(W_t^Q)_{t\geq 0}</math> with values in <math>H</math> is a <math>Q</math>-Wiener process if<ref name=":6" /><ref name=":7">{{Cite book |last=Da Prato |first=Giuseppe |title=Stochastic Equations in Infinite Dimensions |last2=Zabczyk |first2=Jerzy |publisher=[[Cambridge University Press]] |year=2014 |isbn=978-1-107-05584-1 |edition=2nd |pages=81,84}}</ref>

# <math>W_0^Q=0</math>,
# <math>W^Q</math> has continuous trajectories, i.e., for all <math>\omega\in\Omega</math> and <math>t\geq 0</math>
<math>\lim_{s\to t}\lVert W_s(\omega)-W_t(\omega)\rVert=0</math>,
# <math>W^Q</math> has independent increments, i.e., for all <math>0\leq t_1<\dots<t_n</math> and <math>n\in\N</math>
<math>W_{t_1}^Q,\, W_{t_2}^Q-W_{t_1}^Q,\dots,\, W_{t_n}^Q-W_{t_{n-1}}^Q</math> are independent,
# the increments are centered Gaussian, namely <math>W_t^Q-W_s^Q\sim\mathcal N\big(0,(t-s)Q\big)</math> for <math>s<t</math>.

Equivalently, the process can be defined as a series expansion of independent one-dimensional Wiener processes <math>(\beta_k)_{k\in\N}</math> in the basis <math>(e_k)_{k\in\N}</math> of [[Eigenvalues and eigenvectors|eigenvectors]] of <math>Q</math> via<ref name=":6" />

<math display="block">W_t^Q = \sum_{k=1}^\infty\sqrt\lambda_k \beta_k(t) e_k.</math>

This justifies the need to require <math>Q</math> to be trace-class, since

<math display="block">\operatorname E\big[\lVert W_t^Q\rVert^2\big] = t\sum_{k=1}^\infty |\lambda_k|,</math>

which would otherwise diverge.

=== Cylindrical Wiener process ===
The fact that one cannot define a Wiener process on <math>H</math> with covariance operator <math>Q=I</math> (the identity) is unsatisfying. Thus, another approach is required to make sense of

<math display="block">W_t=\sum_{k=1}^\infty\beta_k(t)e_k,</math>

for independent one-dimensional Wiener processes <math>(\beta_k)_{k\in\N}</math> and an orthonormal basis <math>(e_k)_{k\in\N}</math> of <math>H</math>. One possibility consists in evaluating the process only in specific "directions" <math>h\in H</math> in space. For a <math>Q</math>-Wiener process <math>W^Q</math> with a trace class operator <math>Q</math> (which is a well-defined process on <math>H</math>), the projection onto the direction <math>h</math> is

<math display="block">_hW_t^Q:=\langle W_t^Q,h\rangle.</math>

The family <math>(_hW^Q)_{h\in H}</math> is a collection of one-dimensional continuous Gaussian processes with

<math display="block">\begin{align}
&\operatorname E[_hW_t^Q] = 0, \qquad &&\forall h\in H \\
&\operatorname E[_hW_t^Q\, _gW_s^Q] = (t\land s)\langle h,Qg\rangle, \qquad &&\forall h,g\in H.
\end{align}</math>

The above equations still uniquely characterise the process <math>W^Q</math>, but it does not require that <math>Q</math> must be trace class anymore. Thus, going all the way back, a collection <math>(_hW)_{h\in H}</math> of one-dimensional continuous Gaussian processes is called a ''cylindrical Wiener process'' if<ref name=":7" />

<math display="block">\begin{align}
&\operatorname E[_hW_t] = 0, &&\forall h\in H, \\
&\operatorname E[_hW_t\, _gW_s] = (t\land s)\langle h,g\rangle, &&\forall h,g\in H.
\end{align}</math>

This definition does ''not'' define a process <math>W</math> on <math>H</math> with covariance operator <math>Q=I</math>, but the processes <math>_hW</math> behave ''as if'' they were the projections <math>\langle W,h\rangle</math> of the process <math>W</math> if it would exist.

It is also possible to define <math>W</math> by embedding it linearly into another Hilbert space <math>(H_1,\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle_1)</math>, in which the series representation does converge. This can be realised, for example, by taking <math>H_1=H</math>, the embedding <math>J:(H,\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle)\to(H,\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle_1)</math> being the identity and

<math display="block">\langle h, g\rangle_1 := \sum_{k=1}^\infty \frac{1}{k^2}\langle h,e_k\rangle\langle g,e_k\rangle, \quad h,g\in H,</math>

for an orthonormal basis <math>(e_k)_{k\in\N}</math> of <math>H</math> with respect to <math>\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle</math>. In this case,

<math display="block">\tilde W_t := \sum_{k=1}^\infty \beta_k(t) J(e_k) </math>

is a well-defined <math>I</math>-Wiener process on <math>H_1</math>, since

<math display="block">\sum_{k=1}^\infty\langle e_k,Ie_k\rangle_1 = \sum_{k=1}^\infty\frac{1}{k^2}<\infty,</math>

and it is also called a ''cylindrical Wiener process'' on <math>H</math>. Many other pairs of surrogate Hilbert space <math>(H_1,\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle_1)</math> and embedding <math>J</math> are possible for this construction.<ref name=":6" /> 

Once again, <math>\tilde W</math> is not a process on <math>(H,\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle)</math> but on <math>(H_1,\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle_1)</math>, which is either not the space or not the inner product one is interested in. The surrogate Hilbert space <math>(H_1,\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle_1)</math> is merely used as a ground on which <math>\tilde W</math> can be reasonably defined, but due to the injectivity of <math>J</math>, one may think of <math>\tilde W</math> as the unique representative of <math>W</math> on the space <math>(H_1,\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle_1)</math>.

== Related processes ==
[[File:DriftedWienerProcess1D.svg|thumb|Wiener processes with drift ({{color|blue|blue}}) and without drift ({{color|red|red}})]]
[[File:ItoWienerProcess2D.svg|thumb|2D Wiener processes with drift ({{color|blue|blue}}) and without drift ({{color|red|red}})]]
=== Wiener process with drift ===
The stochastic process defined by
<math display="block"> X_t = \mu t + \sigma W_t</math>
for <math>\mu\in\R</math> is called a '''Wiener process with drift μ''' and infinitesimal variance σ<sup>2</sup>>0. These processes exhaust continuous [[Lévy process]]es, which means that they are the only continuous Lévy processes, as a consequence of the Lévy–Khintchine representation. 

=== Brownian bridge ===
Two random processes on the time interval [0, 1] appear, roughly speaking, when conditioning the Wiener process to vanish on both ends of [0,1].  With no further conditioning, the process takes both positive and negative values on [0, 1] and is called [[Brownian bridge]]. Conditioned also to stay positive on (0, 1), the process is called [[Brownian excursion]].<ref>{{cite journal |last=Vervaat |first=W. |year=1979 |title=A relation between Brownian bridge and Brownian excursion |journal=[[Annals of Probability]] |volume=7 |issue=1 |pages=143–149 |jstor=2242845 |doi=10.1214/aop/1176995155|doi-access=free }}</ref> In both cases a rigorous treatment involves a limiting procedure, since the formula ''P''(''A''|''B'') = ''P''(''A'' ∩ ''B'')/''P''(''B'')  does not apply when ''P''(''B'') = 0.

=== Geometric Brownian motion ===
The [[geometric Brownian motion]] is defined as

<math display="block"> S_t = e^{\mu t-\frac{\sigma^2 t}{2}+\sigma W_t}.</math>

It is a stochastic process which is used to model processes that can never take on negative values, such as the value of stocks.

=== Ornstein–Uhlenbeck process ===
The stochastic process
<math display="block">X_t = e^{-t} W_{e^{2t}}</math>
is distributed like the [[Ornstein–Uhlenbeck process]] with parameters <math display="inline">\theta = 1</math>, <math display="inline">\mu = 0</math>, and <math display="inline">\sigma^2 = 2</math>.

=== Integrated Brownian motion ===
The time-integral of the Wiener process
<math display="block">W^{(-1)}_t := \int_0^t W_s \, ds</math>
is called '''integrated Brownian motion''' or '''integrated Wiener process'''. It arises in many applications and can be shown to have the distribution {{math|''N''(0, ''t''<sup>3</sup>/3)}}<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.quantopia.net/interview-questions-vii-integrated-brownian-motion/|title=Interview Questions VII: Integrated Brownian Motion – Quantopia| website=www.quantopia.net| language=en-US| access-date=2017-05-14}}</ref> using [[Fubini's theorem]] and the fact that the covariance of the Wiener process is <math display="inline"> t \wedge s = \min(t, s)</math>.<ref>Forum, [http://wilmott.com/messageview.cfm?catid=4&threadid=39502 "Variance of integrated Wiener process"] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131202222251/http://wilmott.com/messageview.cfm?catid=4&threadid=39502 |date=2013-12-02 }}, 2009.</ref>

A more general process can be defined by 
<math display="block">V_f(t) = \int_0^t f'(s)W_s \,ds=\int_0^t (f(t)-f(s))\,dW_s.</math>
Then, for <math display="inline">a > 0</math>,
<math display="block">\operatorname{Var}(V_f(t))=\int_0^t (f(t)-f(s))^2 \,ds,</math>
<math display="block">\operatorname{cov}(V_f(t+a),V_f(t))=\int_0^t (f(t+a)-f(s))(f(t)-f(s)) \,ds.</math>
In fact, <math display="inline">V_f(t)</math> is always a zero mean normal random variable. This allows for simulation of <math display="inline">V_f(t+a)</math> given <math display="inline">V_f(t)</math> by taking
<math display="block">V_f(t+a)=A\cdot V_f(t) +B\cdot Z</math>
where ''Z'' is a standard normal variable and
<math display="block">A=\frac{\operatorname{cov}(V_f(t+a),V_f(t))}{\operatorname{Var}(V_f(t))},</math>
<math display="block">B^2=\operatorname{Var}(V_f(t+a))-A^2\operatorname{Var}(V_f(t)).</math>
The case of <math display="inline">V_f(t)=W^{(-1)}_t</math> corresponds to <math display="inline">f(t)=t</math>. All these results can be seen as direct consequences of the [[Itô isometry]]. The ''n''-times-integrated Wiener process is a zero-mean normal variable with variance <math display="inline">\frac{t}{2n+1}\left ( \frac{t^n}{n!} \right )^2 </math>. This is given by the [[Cauchy formula for repeated integration]].

=== Process of times to first hitting ===
The [[hitting time|time of hitting]] a single point {{math|''x'' > 0}} by the Wiener process is a random variable with the [[Lévy distribution]]. The family of these random variables (indexed by all positive numbers {{mvar|x}}) is a [[left-continuous]] modification of a [[Lévy process]]. The [[right-continuous]] [[random process|modification]] of this process is given by times of [[hitting time|first exit]] from closed intervals [0, ''x''].{{Citation needed|date=July 2026}}

=== Local time ===
The [[Local time (mathematics)|local time]] {{math|1=''L'' = (''L<sup>x</sup><sub>t</sub>'')<sub>''x'' ∈ '''R''', ''t'' ≥ 0</sub>}} of a Brownian motion describes the time that the process spends at the point {{mvar|x}}. Formally
<math display="block">L^x(t) =\int_0^t \delta(x-W_s)\,ds</math>
where ''δ'' is the [[Dirac delta function]]. The behaviour of the local time is characterized by [[Local time (mathematics)#Ray-Knight Theorems|Ray–Knight theorems]].

=== Brownian martingales ===
A Brownian martingale <math>M</math> is a [[martingale (probability theory)|martingale]] adapted to the Brownian filtration, that is, the [[filtration (probability theory)|filtration]] generated by the Wiener process. Examples for Brownian martingale are <math display="inline">(W_t^2 - t)_{t\geq 0}</math>, the exponential martingale of Brownian motion <math display="inline">(e^{\theta W_t - \tfrac{\theta^2}{2} t})_{t\geq 0}</math> or <math>(\operatorname E[Z\mid W_t])_{t\geq 0}</math> for some integrable random variable <math>Z</math>.<ref name=":1" />

According to the [[martingale representation theorem]], if <math>M</math> is a Brownian martingale adapted to the [[Filtration (probability theory)|augmented]] Brownian filtration and <math>\sup_{t\geq 0}\operatorname E[M_t^2]<\infty</math>, then it can be represented as a stochastic integral of some (unique) process <math>h</math> with <math>\operatorname E\left[\int_0^\infty h_s^2\mathrm d s\right]<\infty</math> against <math>W</math>:<ref name=":1" />

<math display="block">M_t = M_0 + \int_0^t h_s\mathrm d W_s.</math>

In particular, a Brownian martingale with the above properties always has continuous paths.

=== Time change ===
Every adapted continuous local martingale <math>M</math> with <math>M_0=0</math> and diverging [[quadratic variation]] <math>(\langle M \rangle_\infty=\infty)</math> can be expressed as <math>M_t=W_{\langle M\rangle_t}</math> for all <math>t\geq 0</math>. In other words, <math>M</math> is a time changed Wiener process. This is known as the [[Dubins–Schwarz theorem|Dambis–Dubins–Schwarz theorem]]'''.'''<ref name=":1" />

'''Example:'''  {{math|2''W''<sub>''t''</sub> {{=}} ''V''(4''t'')}} where {{mvar|V}} is another Wiener process (different from {{mvar|W}} but distributed like {{mvar|W}}).

'''Example.''' <math display=inline> W_t^2 - t = V_{A(t)} </math> where <math display=inline> A(t) = 4 \int_0^t W_s^2 \, \mathrm{d} s </math> and {{mvar|V}} is another Wiener process.

'''Corollary.''' (See also [[Doob's martingale convergence theorems]]) Let {{math|''M<sub>t</sub>''}} be a continuous martingale, and
<math display="block">M^-_\infty = \liminf_{t\to\infty} M_t,</math>
<math display="block">M^+_\infty = \limsup_{t\to\infty} M_t. </math>

Then only the following two cases are possible:
<math display="block"> -\infty < M^-_\infty = M^+_\infty < +\infty,</math>
<math display="block">-\infty = M^-_\infty < M^+_\infty = +\infty; </math>
other cases (such as <math display="inline"> M^-_\infty = M^+_\infty = +\infty, </math> &nbsp; <math display="inline"> M^-_\infty < M^+_\infty < +\infty </math> etc.) are of probability 0.

Especially, a nonnegative continuous martingale has a finite limit (as ''t'' → ∞) almost surely.

All stated (in this subsection) for martingales holds also for [[local martingale]]s.

=== Change of measure ===
A wide class of [[Semimartingale#Continuous semimartingales|continuous semimartingales]] (especially, of [[diffusion process]]es) is related to the Wiener process via a combination of time change and [[Girsanov theorem|change of measure]].

Using this fact, the [[Wiener process#Qualitative properties|qualitative properties]] stated above for the Wiener process can be generalized to a wide class of continuous semimartingales.<ref name=":2">{{cite book |last1=Revuz |first1=Daniel |last2=Yor |first2=Marc |year=1999 |title=Continuous Martingales and Brownian Motion |edition=3rd |publisher=Springer |series=Grundlehren der mathematischen Wissenschaften |volume=293 |isbn=978-3-540-64325-8|pages=286-287}}</ref><ref>{{cite book |last=Doob |first=J. L. |year=1953 |title=Stochastic Processes |publisher=John Wiley & Sons |location=New York |isbn=978-0471218135}}</ref>

=== Complex-valued Wiener process ===
The complex-valued Wiener process may be defined as a complex-valued random process of the form <math display="inline">Z_t = X_t + i Y_t</math> where <math display="inline">X_t</math> and <math display="inline">Y_t</math> are [[Independence (probability theory)|independent]] Wiener processes (real-valued). In other words, it is the 2-dimensional Wiener process, where we identify <math display="inline">\R^2</math> with <math display="inline">\mathbb C</math>.<ref>{{Citation|title = Estimation of Improper Complex-Valued Random Signals in Colored Noise by Using the Hilbert Space Theory| journal = IEEE Transactions on Information Theory | pages =  2859–2867  | volume = 55 | issue = 6 | doi = 10.1109/TIT.2009.2018329 | last1 = Navarro-moreno | first1 =  J. | last2 =  Estudillo-martinez | first2 =  M.D | last3 =  Fernandez-alcala | first3 =  R.M. | last4 =  Ruiz-molina | first4 =  J.C. |year = 2009 | s2cid = 5911584 }}</ref>

==== Self-similarity ====
Brownian scaling, time reversal, time inversion: the same as in the real-valued case.

Rotation invariance: for every complex number <math display=inline>c</math> such that <math display=inline>|c|=1</math> the process <math display=inline>c \cdot Z_t</math> is another complex-valued Wiener process.

==== Time change ====
If <math display=inline>f</math> is an [[entire function]] then the process <math display=inline> f(Z_t) - f(0) </math> is a time-changed complex-valued Wiener process.

'''Example:''' <math display=inline> Z_t^2 = \left(X_t^2 - Y_t^2\right) + 2 X_t Y_t i = U_{A(t)} </math> where
<math display="block">A(t) = 4 \int_0^t |Z_s|^2 \, \mathrm{d} s </math>
and <math display=inline>U</math> is another complex-valued Wiener process.

In contrast to the real-valued case, a complex-valued martingale is generally not a time-changed complex-valued Wiener process. For example, the martingale <math display=inline>2 X_t + i Y_t</math> is not (here <math display=inline>X_t</math> and <math display=inline>Y_t</math> are independent Wiener processes, as before).

=== Brownian sheet ===
{{main|Brownian sheet}}
The Brownian sheet is a multiparamateric generalization. The definition varies from authors, some define the Brownian sheet to have specifically a two-dimensional time parameter <math display=inline>t</math> while others define it for general dimensions.
